task: Write one sentence of your own using the word potable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know potable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The trail map marks two springs but stars only the northern one as potable; the other is for soaking tired feet.
Usable water will wash a deck or rinse a tool, and that is all it claims; potable sits well above it on this scale — water that has earned the ruling safe to swallow.
Filtered says the water went through a purifier, not that it passed the test; potable is the ruling itself — safe to swallow.

Drinkable is the everyday twin you'd use across a campsite — water you can drink, said casually. Potable is the same verdict in official dress, the word signs, plumbing codes, and ships' logs reach for when the ruling must be exact. Ask a friend if it's drinkable; ask the county if it's potable.

Purified reports a process: the water was cleaned by treatment — boiled, chlorinated, run through membranes. Potable reports a result, safe to swallow, however that result was reached. A mountain spring can be potable with no treatment at all, and sloppily purified water can still fail the test.

The white one is rated potable, so the marina uses it to fill the boats' drinking tanks; the green garden hose leaches enough from its lining that its water is for washing decks and topping off the dinghy — never the kettle.
Potable is a certification, not praise: it says nothing about taste.
Chalky well water can be perfectly potable, and a lovely-looking creek can fail the test by a mile.
The word draws one line — safe to swallow — and stops there; for everything short of the line, English has usable, treated, filtered.
Potable is a certification, not praise: water safe to swallow, whatever it tastes like.
Signs, plumbing codes, and ships' logs use it precisely.
Its unit-mate palatable handles pleasantness — a chalky well can be potable and barely palatable, and a lovely creek can be neither.

After the hurricane, the town's pumps sat underwater for a week, and every tap ran the color of weak tea.
Relief crews rolled in with two kinds of tankers, and the difference between them was painted on the side in tall letters.
Tankers marked potable lined up outside the school; families brought jugs and filled them for cooking, bottles, and coffee.
The unmarked tankers fed a separate line of trucks that flushed hydrants and refilled the hospital's cooling system.
A volunteer kept repeating the rule to every newcomer: if the tanker does not say it in plain letters, nothing from that hose goes near a glass, a kettle, or a toothbrush.
